newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Only police unarmed in Albanian town.
newsitem.headline: Only police unarmed in Albanian town.

text.p: Police in Sarande, a flashpoint of the riots that swept Albania to the brink of anarchy in March, now say they are the only people in the southern town without guns.
"You can't stop crime with your hands in your pockets," Sarande police chief Mustafa Golemi told Reuters. "We need moral and material support from the government."

Golemi's appeal is echoed by police across southern Albania, where a state of generalised lawlessness has followed the riots, which were sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in which many Albanians lost their savings.

"I would be the first to go out with a Kalashnikov and get those criminals if I knew that my wife and children would be looked after," said a senior police officer in nearby Gjirokaster, complaining of lack of support from the Interior Ministry in Tirana.
"We have no support from Tirana, no weapons, nothing," added another officer hitching a lift from the town of Tepelene.

The Interior Ministry is one of just four cabinet portfolios in the nine-party National Reconciliation government still controlled by the Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha. People in the south blame Berisha, a northerner, for the collapse of the pyramid schemes.
The police station and law court in Sarande, a port town close to the Greek border, were burned down in the riots and all the personnel fled.

Looters stole the guns and equipment from the station and destroyed all the police cars. Several military arsenals in the area were broken into, and guns have now been distributed to much of the population.
Golemi, a former army officer, was chosen to rebuild the police force in Sarande by leaders of the local community and his appointment was approved by the Interior Ministry.
He says his men did not arm themselves from the military arsenals "because we are honest men".

The new police force is installed in municipal offices and operates patrols and checkpoints around the town. Police provide guards for all the schools in the town. About 80 per cent of the personnel were police officers before the riots.
Golemi said most of the crime in Sarande is armed robbery, mainly by teenagers who stole guns during the unrest and have no work and little to occupy themselves with.
He is proud of the work his force has done in restoring order after the riots.
"The situation is getting back to normal slowly. There are improvements every day and even at night," he said.
But with so many weapons in the hands of the population, there is huge potential for violence and it is clear that Golemi's force is not fully in control.
"We are functioning as police abandoned by the state and without any assistance," said Golemi's colleague Adrian Luha, the head of public order in the Sarande force.
Golemi says he has been to the Interior Ministry in Tirana four times in the past month, trying in vain to get new equipment.
"We need prosecutors and courts and somewhere to keep prisoners," he said. "Without these things just imagine how hard it is to run a police force."
